analysis.one_liner: Requires US companies with foreign workers to pay a living wage, ban child labor, and meet environmental and human rights standards.
analysis.headline: The Corporate Code of Conduct Act never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in three House committees until Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required any US company employing more than 20 people overseas — directly or through suppliers and subcontractors — to follow a code of conduct: a living wage, no child or forced labor, freedom to unionize, no forced pregnancy testing or birth control, safety rules, environmental standards at least as strong as US law, and respect for international human rights standards. Companies that complied would get preference in federal contracts and in taxpayer-backed export financing and investment insurance; companies found out of compliance could lose those contracts and subsidies. Any member of the public could petition federal agencies to investigate a violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at US-owned or US-controlled factories and suppliers abroad — about 70 percent of them women, according to the bill's findings — would gain wage floors, safety rules, the right to organize, and protection from forced pregnancy testing and firing for reporting abuses. US taxpayers would also gain, since federal contracts, export credits, and investment insurance would flow only to companies meeting the standards.

how_it_helps.text: US companies with more than 20 employees abroad would have to pay a living wage covering a family's basic needs, ban child and forced labor, allow workers to organize and bargain collectively, and prohibit discrimination.

The bill would ban mandatory pregnancy testing, forced use of birth control by employers, and firing or punishing workers for being pregnant — practices the bill says were common among the mostly female workforce in US factories abroad.

The code would extend to partners, suppliers, subcontractors, and even company security forces, and companies would have to publicly disclose factory locations, working conditions, and environmental performance.

Federal agencies would have to prefer code-compliant companies in contracting, and the Export-Import Bank, Overseas Private Investment Corporation, and Trade and Development Agency would have to prefer them in export financing and investment insurance; agencies could terminate contracts of noncompliant firms.

Any person could petition Commerce, Labor, State, or the EPA to investigate alleged violations, with a required investigation unless the petition is frivolous, a public hearing, a decision within 270 days, and court review.

analysis.who_pays: US multinational companies and their suppliers would bear the cost of raising wages to living-wage levels, ending practices like forced pregnancy testing, upgrading environmental controls to US-equivalent standards, and running internal compliance programs. Firms that lose federal contracts or export financing over violations would bear those losses too.

drawbacks.text: Compliance monitoring is left largely to a self-financing program inside each company, so the burden of detecting violations would rest heavily on the firms being regulated.

Because the rules apply only to US nationals, they could raise costs for US companies relative to foreign competitors operating in the same countries, potentially pushing some production toward firms outside the reach of the law.
Determining a 'living wage' through wage studies in dozens of countries, and monitoring suppliers and subcontractors down the chain, would be administratively complex and open to dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — a living wage, basic labor rights, and environmental protection for workers abroad, plus tighter conditions on taxpayer-backed corporate support — are substantial and targeted at real, documented abuses. The costs fall on the companies creating those conditions, though the one-chamber-only, US-firms-only design could shift some problems to foreign competitors rather than eliminate them, and self-policing is a weak enforcement backbone.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to four subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Cynthia McKinney introduced the bill on June 7, 2000, joined by 14 original cosponsors including Bernie Sanders, Dennis Kucinich, and Barney Frank-era progressives such as Peter DeFazio and Jerrold Nadler.
The House referred it simultaneously to the International Relations, Government Reform, and Banking and Financial Services committees, with no committee given clear lead jurisdiction.
Between June 19 and July 17, 2000, it was further referred to four subcommittees; the record shows no hearings, no markup, and no vote in any of them.
It ended the Congress with 32 cosponsors — 31 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republican support and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational companies came out ahead: they kept their existing overseas labor, environmental, and disclosure practices, and continued receiving federal contracts, export financing, and investment insurance without conditions on how they treated foreign workers.

industries.industry: US multinational manufacturers with overseas supply chains
industries.note: The bill would have required living wages, union rights, an end to forced pregnancy testing, and US-equivalent environmental standards across their foreign operations and supplier chains. Their cost savings from the status quo came at the expense of workers abroad and communities near their plants.

industries.industry: Recipients of federal contracts and export financing (Ex-Im Bank, OPIC, TDA)
industries.note: Compliant firms would gain a leg up in federal contracts and taxpayer-backed export credit and investment insurance, but any firm found out of compliance could have its contract or assistance terminated. The bill would have made continued access to public money conditional on conduct abroad.

industries.industry: Corporate security and subcontractor firms abroad
industries.note: Security forces and subcontractors would be explicitly brought under the code by contract, ending their exemption from the conduct standards applied to the parent company.
